title: Comparing Without Full Calculation
sub: Compare fractions, roots and powers the smart way

steps.html:
Compare, Don't Calculate

You only need to know which is bigger, not the exact values.

516 vs 310cross-multiply: 5 × 10 = 50 vs 3 × 16 = 48
50 > 48so 516 is bigger
say: Today: comparing quantities without doing all the math.
On comparison questions, you only need to know which is bigger, not exact values.
To compare two fractions, cross-multiply. Five times ten is fifty. Three times sixteen is forty-eight. Fifty is bigger, so five sixteenths is bigger.
Which is bigger, four sevenths or five ninths?
steps.okSay: Yes! Four times nine is thirty-six, five times seven is thirty-five. Four sevenths wins.
steps.noSay: Not quite. Cross-multiply: four times nine is thirty-six, five times seven is thirty-five. Four sevenths is bigger.

steps.html:
Square roots: compare the squares

√110 vs 10.6
Square both: 110 vs 10.6² = 112.36
110 < 112.36, so √110 < 10.6
say: Comparing a square root with a decimal? Square both.
Root one-ten versus ten point six.
Square both sides. One-ten stays one-ten. Ten point six squared is one twelve point three six.
One-ten is smaller, so root one-ten is smaller.

steps.html:
Fractions between 0 and 1 shrink when powered

(34)2 = 916smaller than 34
number > 1squared gets bigger
0 and 1stay the same
say: Here's a surprise. Square a fraction between zero and one, and it gets smaller. Three fourths squared is nine sixteenths, which is less than three fourths.
Numbers bigger than one get bigger when squared. And zero and one stay exactly the same.
Quantity A is two thirds squared. Quantity B is two thirds. Which is greater?
steps.ok: Yes! A fraction between 0 and 1 gets smaller when squared: 4/9 < 6/9.
steps.okSay: Yes! Squaring a fraction between zero and one makes it smaller.
steps.noSay: Not quite. Two thirds squared is four ninths, which is less than six ninths. B is greater.

steps.html:
Same parts? Cancel them.

A: 47 × 23 + 15   B: 47 × 23 + 18
Both have 47 × 23. Ignore it: 15 vs 18 → B
say: Another trick: if both sides share the same piece, cross it out.
Both quantities have forty-seven times twenty-three. Ignore it. Fifteen versus eighteen: B wins, and you never multiplied.
Great! Now 4 practice questions. You'll see the answer and an explanation after each one.
Last part: three checkpoint questions. Get two out of three to finish the lesson. You've got this!

steps.html:
Remember

1. Fractions: cross-multiply to compare.

2. Roots vs decimals: square both.

3. Between 0 and 1: powers make it smaller.

4. Same piece on both sides? Cross it out.
say: Let's review. Compare fractions by cross-multiplying.
Compare a root with a decimal by squaring both.
Fractions between zero and one get smaller when you square them.
And when both sides share a piece, cross it out. Great work!
